blocks.text: The 'Double-Dip' Storm Cycle: Paying Twice for One Weather Event

In commercial janitorial contracts across the 2,500 to 24,999 square foot brackets ($0.07 to $0.15 per square foot per visit), monthly billing is almost universally structured as a flat 1/12th annual retainer using the 4.33 weeks-per-month multiplier (21.65 visits per month for 5x/week service at the 0.90 frequency multiplier, or 13.0 visits per month for 3x/week service at the 0.95 multiplier). When a severe winter blizzard, ice storm, or hurricane sweeps through your region, a poorly drafted contract allows the janitorial vendor to profit twice from the same disruption.

First, the contractor invoices 100% of the fixed monthly retainer even though their night crew stayed home for two or three nights during the storm. Second, when employees return and track rock salt, sand, and slush across the lobby and elevator landings, the vendor declares the heavy residue 'outside routine daily scope' and presents an emergency work order billed at inflated restoration rates. Avoiding these billing traps mistakes snow and storm cleanup contingency clauses requires dissecting what vendor-drafted agreements deliberately leave out.
Mistake 1: Relying on Standard Boilerplate 'Force Majeure' Language

Most commercial cleaning agreements contain a generic Force Majeure paragraph stating that neither party shall be liable for delays or failures to perform caused by 'Acts of God, severe weather, floods, or governmental orders.' Facility managers often read that sentence and assume it protects them. In legal and accounting reality, a standard Force Majeure clause merely excuses the janitorial company from breach-of-contract damages when they fail to show up during a snowstorm—it does NOT automatically reduce your fixed monthly payment obligation.

Unless your contract explicitly pairs Force Majeure with a 'Proportionate Fee Abatement or Hour Banking' sub-clause, accounts payable must still pay the full monthly invoice while your facility goes uncleaned.
Mistake 2: Allowing Unilateral Vendor 'Safety Cancellations' Without Audit Criteria

Another silent loophole appears when a vendor's proposal states: 'Contractor reserves the right to suspend night operations whenever road conditions are deemed hazardous by Contractor supervision, without penalty.' When labor is tight on a Friday evening with 1 inch of light snow on suburban roads—even though your office was open all day and no municipal travel advisory exists—an understaffed vendor can invoke unilateral weather suspension to skip your building, save 8 hours of $35 to $65/hour payroll, and pocket the retainer.

blocks.text: Mistake 3: Failing to Draw Down Banked Hours Before Paying 'Emergency Salt Cleanup' Invoices

Even when a facility manager negotiates an 'hour bank' for snow days, billing leaks happen if the accounting workflow isn't tight. Suppose a Tuesday blizzard closes your 20,000-square-foot office, banking 5.71 standard labor hours (calculated at the ISSA 3,500 sq ft/hr benchmark). On Wednesday night, the crew returns and spends 4 extra man-hours wet-extracting slush from entrance walk-off mats and auto-scrubbing calcium chloride rings off VCT corridors (1.04x multiplier) and polished concrete lobbies (0.95x multiplier).

blocks.title: Watch Out for Separate 'Special Services' Invoices After a Storm
blocks.text: Many national and regional janitorial software platforms auto-generate a separate Time & Materials invoice from the 'Special Projects Division' whenever a crew logs extra floor extraction hours—even when your regular monthly contract owes you 6 to 12 hours of banked snow-day credit. Require that all post-storm extra labor automatically draw down your banked closure balance to zero before a single dollar of T&M ($55 to $95/hr specialty rate) can be invoiced.
Mistake 4: Neglecting Post-Storm Disinfection and Cross-Contamination Protocols

Storm recoveries aren't limited to winter snow. Heavy summer thunderstorms, tropical depressions, and rapid snowmelt frequently trigger minor ground-level seepage, backed-up floor drains in basement restrooms ($15 to $30 per restroom per visit), or damp wind-blown debris at loading dock entrances. A critical mistake is allowing janitorial crews to wipe down storm-soiled entrance sills, breakrooms ($12 to $25/visit), and restroom floors using the same mop water or uncoded rags, spreading outdoor street runoff and bacteria onto office touchpoints.

Your storm contingency exhibit should specify the exact sanitation chemistry and color-coded wiping media required during post-weather recovery shifts. For sanitizing floor drains, ceramic tile restrooms (1.12x multiplier), and storm-water intrusion zones, mandate the Diversey Virex II 256 One-Step Disinfectant Cleaner Gallon, which provides a 1 gal container with an economical 1:256 Yield, Neutral pH finish compatibility, and Hospital Grade quaternary disinfection. For daily wipe-downs of mud-splashed kickplates, reception counters, and breakroom surfaces, specify the ECOS Pro Orange Plus All-Purpose Cleaner (1-Gallon), offering a 1 gal capacity with EPA Safer Choice certification, Plant-Based surfactants, and Low VOC indoor air compliance. To prevent crews from transferring floor slush residue onto desks or glass partitions ($15 to $35/visit), require the Microfiber Wholesale 16x16 Commercial Cleaning Cloths (150-Pack, Color-Coded), which supplies 150 Cloths in a 16x16 in size with high-absorbency 300 GSM weave and an OSHA-aligned 4-Color Code system (red for restrooms, yellow for glass, blue for general office, and green for breakroom kitchenettes).
Checklist: 4 Clauses to Add Before Signing Your Next Janitorial Renewal

items: Mutual Closure Definition: Excused weather closures require either an official municipal travel restriction, landlord building shutdown, or written client instruction delivered at least 4 hours prior to shift start.

Automatic Credit or 60-Day Rollover Election: Give the Facility Manager—not the vendor—the sole option to elect either a pro-rata invoice credit (Monthly Fee / 21.65 for 5x/week) or 1:1 banked deep-cleaning hours expiring after 60 days.

Mandatory Salt-Neutralizer Window: Require pH-neutralizing floor rinse solutions on all hard floors and entrance carpet extraction zones from November 1 through April 15 as part of the base per-square-foot price.
Pre-Locked Emergency Rate Cap: Cap any authorized emergency storm water extraction beyond banked hours at $55 to $95 per man-hour, with zero unapproved third-party subcontractor markups.

faqs.q: Can a cleaning company refuse to issue a credit for a snow day if our office was officially closed?
faqs.a: If you signed a lump-sum monthly contract without an explicit weather abatement or visit-credit clause, the vendor will often argue that the agreement is an outcomes-based monthly retainer rather than a per-visit contract. To prevent this, always define your monthly fee in the contract Pricing Schedule as a unit rate per visit multiplied by 21.65 visits/month (5x/week), 13.0 visits/month (3x/week), or 8.66 visits/month (2x/week) based on 4.33 weeks/month.

faqs.q: Why does mopping winter salt with standard floor cleaner ruin VCT and hardwood floors?
faqs.a: Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride ice melters leave an alkaline film with a pH between 9.0 and 10.5. Mopping with plain water or an alkaline all-purpose cleaner simply spreads the dissolved salt across the floor; as the water evaporates, the salt recrystallizes into a chalky white haze that etches acrylic VCT wax (1.04x multiplier) and dulls urethane hardwood coatings (1.08x multiplier). An organic acid salt-neutralizer is required to dissolve and lift the mineral bond.

faqs.q: What is a fair notice window for cancelling a janitorial shift ahead of an incoming storm?
faqs.a: Four hours prior to the scheduled shift start time (for example, notifying the account manager by 2:00 PM for a 6:00 PM night shift) is the US commercial industry standard. If an afternoon storm forces an emergency closure with less than 4 hours notice and technicians have already reported to the site, a fair contract permits a 2-hour show-up fee ($70 to $130 per worker at $35 to $65/hr) while crediting or banking the remaining shift hours.

faqs.q: Should our janitorial vendor handle exterior sidewalk snow shoveling and salting under the same clause?
faqs.a: Only if exterior grounds maintenance is explicitly priced in a separate Snow & Ice Removal Addendum with dedicated slip-and-fall General Liability coverage (COI endorsement for snow/ice operations). Most indoor janitorial policies exclude exterior sidewalk snow clearing beyond sweeping immediate covered entrance thresholds; mixing the two without verifying COI endorsements creates serious slip-and-fall liability exposure.
